stem: Which feature is most characteristic of a steroid hormone acting on its target cell?
choices: It binds an intracellular receptor
It is stored in secretory vesicles
It binds a cell surface receptor
It acts only through cyclic AMP
It has a very short half-life
ex: Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone) are made from cholesterol as needed, diffuse out of the cell, travel bound to proteins and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11). (Exam 1 · L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary)
why: Steroids diffuse into the target cell and bind intracellular (nuclear) receptors that change gene transcription.
That is a peptide hormone; steroids aren't stored but diffuse out of the cell as they are made.
Peptides and catecholamines use cell surface receptors; steroids cross the membrane.
cAMP is a second messenger of some surface receptors (Gs); steroid receptors act on genes.
Steroids ride the blood bound to binding proteins rather than free; a short half-life isn't their hallmark.

likely.t: L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): a steroid hormone binds an intracellular receptor; and its twin, the peptide's surface receptor

stem: Which feature is most characteristic of a peptide hormone acting on its target cell?
choices: It binds a cell surface receptor
It is stored in secretory vesicles
It binds an intracellular receptor
It acts only through cyclic AMP
It has a very short half-life
ex: Peptide hormones are made as large preprohormones, stored in secretory vesicles until a rise in intracellular calcium releases them, travel mostly free and act through cell surface receptors. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on steroid hormones, with a different answer. (Exam 1 · L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary)
why: Peptides can't cross the membrane, so they bind receptors on the target cell's surface (often G-protein-coupled).
True of peptides, but in the cell that makes them, before release, not at the target cell.
That is the steroid (and thyroid hormone) pattern.
Surface receptors use more than one messenger: Gs raises cAMP, Gi lowers it, Gq raises IP3 and calcium.
Peptides travel mostly free in the blood, but the feature that defines how they act on the target is the surface receptor.

likely.t: L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): a steroid hormone binds an intracellular receptor; and its twin, the peptide's surface receptor

stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has marked insulin resistance. Which drug improves insulin sensitivity through activation of PPAR-gamma?
choices: Pioglitazone
Glimepiride
Repaglinide
Sitagliptin
Dapagliflozin
ex: Pioglitazone (Actos) and rosiglitazone (Avandia) are thiazolidinediones, PPAR-gamma agonists. PPAR-gamma is a nuclear receptor, mostly in adipose tissue, that switches on genes of glucose and lipid metabolism, and insulin sensitivity improves. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11).
why: A thiazolidinedione: a PPAR-gamma agonist that improves insulin sensitivity.
A second-generation sulfonylurea: it closes K-ATP channels and releases insulin.
A meglitinide: it works on the same K-ATP channel as the sulfonylureas.
A DPP-4 inhibitor: it makes the body's own incretins last longer.
An SGLT2 inhibitor: it blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney.

stem: Which of these drugs is a second-generation sulfonylurea that releases insulin by closing K-ATP channels on beta cells?
choices: Glimepiride
Pioglitazone
Repaglinide
Sitagliptin
Dapagliflozin
ex: The insulin secretagogues close K-ATP channels on the beta cell: the sulfonylureas (second generation: glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride) and the meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide), which share two binding sites with them. Every drug that releases insulin causes hypoglycemia and weight gain. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on pioglitazone, with a different answer.
why: A second-generation sulfonylurea, with glyburide and glipizide: it closes K-ATP channels, so the beta cell releases insulin.
A thiazolidinedione (PPAR-gamma agonist): it improves insulin sensitivity and doesn't release insulin.

A DPP-4 inhibitor: it raises the body's own incretins.
An SGLT2 inhibitor: glucose leaves in the urine, with no insulin release.

stem: Which insulin analog is best classified as a rapid-acting insulin used for mealtime glucose control?
choices: Insulin lispro
Insulin degludec
Insulin glargine
NPH insulin
Regular insulin

Ultra-long-acting: lasts more than 42 hours, used as basal insulin.
Long-acting: slow, steady release with no real peak, more than 24 hours; basal, once daily.
Intermediate-acting human insulin: onset 2 to 4 hours, slowed by protamine.
Short-acting human insulin, not an analog: peaks at about 3 hours, gone by about 8.

Insulin degludec

Insulin lispro

Increasing renal glucose loss
Increasing pancreatic glucagon
Activating PPAR-gamma receptors
Blocking intestinal DPP-4

why: Metformin's primary effect is to inhibit hepatic gluconeogenesis; it also improves peripheral insulin sensitivity.

stem: Inhibition of DPP-4 improves glycemic control primarily by prolonging the action of which endogenous hormones?
choices: Incretin hormones
Catecholamines
Glucocorticoids
Mineralocorticoids
Thyroid hormones

why: DPP-4 breaks down the body's own GLP-1 and GIP; blocking it lets the incretins made after each meal last longer.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine aren't the hormones DPP-4 breaks down.

Not DPP-4 substrates.

Retinopathy
Nephropathy
Peripheral neuropathy

Microvascular.
Microvascular.

stem: The most common functioning pituitary adenoma primarily secretes which hormone?
choices: Prolactin
Growth hormone
ACTH
TSH
Oxytocin

Somatotroph adenomas cause gigantism or acromegaly; they are the largest, not the most common.

ACTH
TSH
Prolactin

stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism?
choices: High calcium, low phosphate
Low calcium, high phosphate
Low calcium, low phosphate
High calcium, high phosphate
Normal calcium, high phosphate
ex: Primary hyperparathyroidism is PTH secretion inappropriately high for the serum calcium, with the gland itself the problem (an adenoma in 80 to 90 percent). Dr. Dababneh's shorthand: PTH takes back calcium and dumps phosphate, so calcium is high and phosphate low. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11).
why: Too much PTH: calcium comes out of bone and is held by the kidney, and phosphate is dumped in the urine.
Too little PTH effect: hypoparathyroidism or pseudohypoparathyroidism.
Calcium is low, so PTH isn't in excess; in primary disease calcium rises.
PTH makes the kidney dump phosphate, so phosphate falls, not rises.
Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium and lowers phosphate.

stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with hypoparathyroidism after the parathyroids were removed along with the thyroid?
choices: Low calcium, high phosphate
High calcium, low phosphate
Low calcium, low phosphate
High calcium, high phosphate
Normal calcium, high phosphate
ex: Hypoparathyroidism is low serum calcium due to underproduction of PTH; surgery (a thyroidectomy that takes the parathyroids) is one of its three groups of causes. Pseudohypoparathyroidism looks the same, low calcium and high phosphate, but PTH is high. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on primary hyperparathyroidism, with a different answer.
why: No PTH: calcium isn't pulled from bone or held by the kidney, and phosphate isn't dumped.

Without PTH the kidney keeps phosphate, so it rises.
Without PTH, calcium falls.

Persistent hypoglycemia
Reduced hepatic glucose output
Reduced protein catabolism
Increased insulin sensitivity

why: Cortisol is the "sugar" hormone of the zona fasciculata: Cushing syndrome brings hyperglycemia.

stem: Which finding is most consistent with the cortisol and aldosterone deficiency of Addison disease?
choices: Low blood glucose
Elevated blood glucose
High serum sodium
Low serum potassium
High blood pressure

why: Without cortisol, glucose is low, with fatigue and weakness.
That is cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome).
Without aldosterone, sodium is low.
Without aldosterone, potassium is high.
Without aldosterone, blood pressure is low.

Stimulate pituitary LH release
Promote testosterone breakdown
Trigger sperm ejaculation
Convert testosterone to DHT
ex: Under FSH, Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein, which binds testosterone and keeps it highly concentrated in the tubules; the developing sperm depend on that strong signal. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11).
why: ABP binds testosterone and keeps it highly concentrated in the tubules, higher than in the blood.
Testosterone lowers LH; ABP doesn't act on the pituitary.
It holds testosterone in the tubule rather than breaking it down.
Ejaculation is a sympathetic reflex ("shoot").
That is 5-alpha-reductase.

stem: What is the principal role of 5-alpha-reductase in the penis, scrotum and prostate?
choices: Convert testosterone to DHT
Stimulate pituitary LH release
Promote testosterone breakdown
Trigger sperm ejaculation
Maintain high local testosterone
ex: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in the tissues that are more sensitive to DHT, which express a lot of the enzyme: the penis, scrotum and prostate. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on androgen-binding protein, with a different answer.
why: These tissues are more sensitive to DHT and express a lot of 5-alpha-reductase, so testosterone that reaches them becomes DHT.
An enzyme in the target tissues, not a signal to the pituitary.
It turns testosterone into DHT, the androgen these tissues respond to, not into an inactive product.
Ejaculation is a sympathetic reflex.
That is androgen-binding protein, in the tubules.

Parasympathetic division
Enteric nervous system
Somatic sensory system
Central vagal system

why: "Point and Shoot": S for shoot, sympathetic, the emission and ejaculation.
P for point: the erection and lubrication.
The gut's own nervous system, not the sexual response.
Not an autonomic division; the lecture gives the climax to the sympathetic division.
The vagus is parasympathetic, and the lecture gives emission to the sympathetic division.

stem: Which hormone is normally dominant during the luteal phase of the ovarian cycle?
choices: Progesterone
FSH
LH
Estradiol
Prolactin
ex: Follicular phase (days 0 to 14): the growing follicle, 17-beta estradiol dominant. Luteal phase (days 14 to 28): the corpus luteum, progesterone dominant, with negative feedback on GnRH, LH and FSH. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11).
why: The corpus luteum makes progesterone at much higher levels in the luteal phase.
Progesterone's negative feedback holds FSH down in the luteal phase.
LH surges at midcycle; in the luteal phase progesterone holds it down.
Dominant in the follicular phase; the corpus luteum still makes some.
Not a cycle hormone in the lecture; high prolactin turns GnRH down.

stem: Which hormone is normally dominant during the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle?
choices: Estradiol
FSH
LH
Progesterone
Prolactin
ex: Comparing the two phases is "high yield for exam": the follicular phase is driven by the growing follicle, with estradiol dominant; the luteal phase by the corpus luteum, with progesterone dominant. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on the luteal phase, with a different answer.
why: The growing follicle makes 17-beta estradiol, the follicular phase's dominant hormone.
FSH starts the follicles growing, but estradiol is the phase's dominant hormone.
LH surges at midcycle, at the end of the follicular phase.
Dominant in the luteal phase, from the corpus luteum.
Not a cycle hormone in the lecture; high prolactin turns GnRH down.

5-alpha-reductase
Cholesterol desmolase
21-hydroxylase
Tyrosine hydroxylase

why: FSH makes granulosa cells express and activate aromatase, which converts testosterone to 17-beta estradiol.
It converts testosterone to DHT, in male tissues.
The rate-limiting step, raised by LH in the theca cells.
An adrenal enzyme on the way to cortisol and aldosterone; he only wants aromatase and cholesterol desmolase.

choices: Cholesterol desmolase
5-alpha-reductase
21-hydroxylase
Aromatase
Tyrosine hydroxylase

They have no aromatase, so the granulosa cells finish the job. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on aromatase, with a different answer.
why: LH raises cholesterol desmolase (P450scc), which turns cholesterol into pregnenolone: the rate-limiting step.
It converts testosterone to DHT, in male tissues.
An adrenal enzyme on the way to cortisol and aldosterone, not the theca cell's.
FSH raises aromatase in the granulosa cells; theca cells have none.
It makes catecholamines, not steroids.

stem: Sustained high estradiol levels just before ovulation produce which effect on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis?
choices: Positive feedback promoting an LH surge
Suppression of all GnRH release
Inhibition of ovarian FSH receptors
Loss of pituitary LH receptors
Direct secretion of progesterone
ex: Estrogen gives both kinds of feedback: at ordinary levels it suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH, but as estradiol keeps rising it progressively sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH, so just before ovulation GnRH sets off a burst of LH. That positive feedback is what makes the female axis cyclical. From the Exam 2 in-class review (PollEv, 11/11).
why: Rising estradiol sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH, so it releases a burst of LH.
Ordinary estradiol levels give negative feedback; high levels at midcycle switch to positive.
Not an effect on the axis; inhibin is what holds FSH down.
Estradiol makes the pituitary more responsive to GnRH, not less.
Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum, after ovulation.

stem: During the luteal phase, what effect does progesterone from the corpus luteum have on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis?
choices: Negative feedback on GnRH, LH and FSH
Positive feedback promoting an LH surge
Inhibition of ovarian FSH receptors
Loss of pituitary LH receptors
Direct secretion of estradiol
ex: Progesterone gives negative feedback only, on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary; estrogen is negative most of the time and positive at one point, the middle of the cycle. A twin of the Exam 2 review question on estradiol's positive feedback, with a different answer.
why: Progesterone is "always going to be negative feedback," on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary.
That is high estradiol, just before ovulation.
Not an effect on the axis.
Not what progesterone does; it lowers GnRH, LH and FSH.
The corpus luteum still makes some estradiol, but that isn't an effect on the axis.

stem: Which two hormones work synergistically to raise blood calcium?
choices: PTH and calcitriol (active vitamin D)
PTH and calcitonin
Calcitonin and calcitriol
PTH and 24,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (24,25-(OH)2-D3)
ex: PTH and vitamin D work synergistically: PTH stimulates 1α-hydroxylase in the kidney, and the calcitriol it makes raises calcium absorption in the gut (the channels, calbindin and the basolateral pump), while PTH itself frees calcium from bone and holds it at the kidney. (Exam 1 · L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation)
why: PTH turns on the kidney's 1α-hydroxylase, and the calcitriol it makes raises calcium absorption in the gut: PTH and vitamin D work synergistically.
Calcitonin, from the thyroid's C cells, inhibits osteoclasts and lowers calcium; it works against PTH.
Calcitonin lowers blood calcium, so it is no partner in raising it.
The 24,25 form is the inactive one the kidney's 24-hydroxylase makes; PTH turns on 1α-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol.

likely.t: L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: Which hormones synergize: PTH and vitamin D (calcitriol) raise blood calcium together

stem: How does PTH increase calcium absorption from the gut?
choices: Through renal 1α-hydroxylase and calcitriol
By acting directly on enterocytes
By inhibiting calcitonin
By increasing gastrin secretion
ex: PTH stimulates 1α-hydroxylase; calcitriol then raises gut absorption. PTH and vitamin D work synergistically. (Exam 1 · L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation)
why: Through more active vitamin D.
PTH acts on the gut indirectly.
Not the mechanism.
Gastrin stimulates calcitonin.

likely.t: L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: Which hormones synergize: PTH and vitamin D (calcitriol) raise blood calcium together

stem: Blood calcium falls and PTH rises. How does PTH bring calcium back to normal?
choices: It frees calcium from bone, holds it at the kidney and, through calcitriol, raises gut absorption
It acts directly on intestinal cells to absorb more calcium, and on osteoclasts through their own PTH receptor
It holds calcium at the kidney only, with no effect on bone or the gut
It makes the kidney keep phosphate along with the calcium
ex: PTH answers low calcium at all three sites: bone (its receptor is on the osteoblasts, which signal the osteoclasts to resorb), the kidney (keep calcium, dump phosphate, and turn on 1α-hydroxylase) and, through the calcitriol that makes, the gut. The net effect is calcium up, phosphate down. (Exam 1 · L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation)
why: All three sites: bone through osteoblasts, the kidney (keep calcium, dump phosphate, turn on 1α-hydroxylase) and the gut through calcitriol.
Its gut effect is indirect, through calcitriol, and its bone receptor is on osteoblasts, which signal the osteoclasts; osteoclasts have no PTH receptor.
The kidney is one of three sites: PTH also acts on bone and, through calcitriol, on the gut.
PTH dumps phosphate in the urine, so blood phosphate falls: net calcium up, phosphate down.

likely.t: L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: How PTH maintains blood calcium: bone, the kidney, and the gut through calcitriol; calcium up, phosphate down

stem: The net effect of PTH on blood is:
choices: Calcium up, phosphate down
Calcium up, phosphate up
Calcium down, phosphate up
Calcium down, phosphate down
ex: Bone resorption releases both, but renal phosphate excretion wins: calcium rises, phosphate falls. (Exam 1 · L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation)
why: Ca up, P down.
Phosphate is excreted.
That is the opposite of PTH.
Calcium rises.

likely.t: L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: How PTH maintains blood calcium: bone, the kidney, and the gut through calcitriol; calcium up, phosphate down

stem: Which hormone works synergistically with GH on bone growth in children?
choices: Thyroid hormone (T3)
Somatostatin
High-dose glucocorticoids
Aldosterone
ex: In children thyroid hormone acts synergistically with growth hormone on bone, stimulating chondrocytes, osteoblasts and osteoclasts and keeping the ossification centers active; T3 sits on the growth plate slide with GH and IGF-1. (Exam 1 · L3 Endocrinology of Growth)
why: It sits with GH and IGF-1 on the growth plate slide and acts synergistically with GH on bone.
Somatostatin, through Gi, lowers GH release; it works against GH, not with it.
High-dose glucocorticoids stunt growth in children; they work against GH.
Aldosterone keeps sodium and loses potassium; it has no role at the growth plate.

choices: True
False

stem: Which statement about how long the insulins act is true?
choices: Regular insulin peaks at about 3 hours and is gone by about 8 hours
Lispro, aspart and glulisine start in 5 to 15 minutes and last about 12 hours
Glargine lasts more than 24 hours, with a sharp peak at about 6 hours
Inhaled Afrezza starts acting in about 2 to 4 hours, like NPH
ex: Rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset 5 to 15 minutes, about 4 hours. Regular: peak about 3 hours, gone by 8. NPH: onset 2 to 4 hours. Glargine: more than 24 hours, no peak; degludec more than 42 hours. Afrezza (inhaled): 1 to 2 minutes.
why: Regular (short-acting) insulin peaks around 3 hours and wears off by about 8.
The rapid insulins do start in 5 to 15 minutes, but they last about 4 hours, not 12.
Glargine is the peakless basal insulin: more than 24 hours with no peak.
The 2 to 4 hour onset is NPH's; Afrezza starts in 1 to 2 minutes.

stem: Which statement about acarbose and miglitol is true?
choices: They block brush-border alpha-glucosidase, so flatulence and bloating are common
They block brush-border alpha-glucosidase, and hypoglycemia is their main adverse effect
They block the SGLT2 transporter in the kidney, so flatulence and bloating are common
They close the beta cell K-ATP channel, so flatulence and bloating are common
ex: Acarbose and miglitol block alpha-glucosidase at the intestinal brush border, so carbohydrate is absorbed more slowly. The undigested sugar ferments in the colon (flatulence, bloating, diarrhea), and they cause no hypoglycemia on their own.
why: Undigested carbohydrate reaches the colon and ferments: flatulence, bloating and diarrhea.
On their own they cause no hypoglycemia; their adverse effects are in the gut.
Blocking SGLT2 is what the gliflozins do; acarbose and miglitol act in the gut.
Closing the K-ATP channel is how sulfonylureas release insulin.

stem: Which statement about the thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) is false?
choices: They are safe to start in NYHA class III or IV heart failure
They act on PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor
They can cause edema, weight gain and macular edema
They are avoided when ALT is over 2.5 times the upper limit of normal
ex: TZDs act on PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor. Their problems come from fluid retention: edema, weight gain, heart failure and macular edema. Avoid them in NYHA class III and IV heart failure and when ALT is over 2.5 times normal.
why: This is the false one: they cause fluid retention and are avoided in NYHA class III and IV heart failure.
This is true: TZDs are PPAR-gamma agonists, and PPAR-gamma is a nuclear receptor.
This is true: fluid retention drives the edema, weight gain, heart failure and macular edema.
This is true: the lecture gives ALT over 2.5 times normal as a reason not to use them.

stem: Which statement about the sulfonylureas is false?
choices: They lower glucose even in a patient with no working beta cells
They close the beta cell K-ATP channel, so calcium enters and insulin is released
Patients with G6PD deficiency need caution with them
Taken with alcohol, they can cause a disulfiram-like reaction
ex: Sulfonylureas close the beta cell K-ATP channel: depolarization, calcium in, insulin out. They need working beta cells, and as those fail the dose climbs until the drug stops working. Warnings: G6PD deficiency, liver and kidney disease, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
why: This is the false one: they work by making beta cells release insulin, so they need working beta cells.
This is true: closing the channel depolarizes the cell, calcium enters and insulin is released.
This is true: G6PD deficiency is one of the lecture's sulfonylurea warnings.
This is true: flushing, nausea and headache with alcohol, a disulfiram-like reaction.

stem: Which statement about pituitary adenomas is true?
choices: Gonadotroph adenomas cause no hormone syndrome and are found by their mass effect
Prolactinomas are the least common hyperfunctioning pituitary tumor
Somatotroph adenomas are usually the smallest pituitary adenomas, most under 10 mm across
A microadenoma is over 10 mm across and a macroadenoma is under 10 mm
ex: Prolactinoma: the most common hyperfunctioning type, usually a microadenoma. Somatotroph: the largest. Gonadotroph: no syndrome, found by mass effect. Micro means under 10 mm, macro over 10 mm.
why: Gonadotroph adenomas make FSH and LH but have no clinical syndrome, so they surface as macroadenomas through mass effect.
Prolactinomas are the most common hyperfunctioning pituitary tumor.
Somatotroph adenomas are the largest, and mass effects are frequent.
That swaps them: a microadenoma is under 10 mm, a macroadenoma over 10 mm.

stem: Which statement about how thyroid carcinomas spread is true?
choices: Papillary carcinoma spreads by lymphatics; follicular carcinoma spreads by blood
Papillary carcinoma spreads by blood; follicular carcinoma spreads by lymphatics
Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood, and its usual targets are the liver and spleen
Papillary carcinoma spreads by lymphatics and is usually a single focus in one lobe
ex: Papillary: lymphatics to the lymph nodes, often multifocal (total thyroidectomy). Follicular: capsular or vascular invasion and spread by blood to the lung and bone.
why: Papillary goes to the lymph nodes; follicular invades vessels and spreads by blood.
That swaps them: papillary is the lymphatic one, follicular the one that travels by blood.
Follicular carcinoma does spread by blood, but to the lung and bone.
Papillary carcinoma is often multifocal, which is why the whole thyroid comes out.

stem: Which statement about Graves disease is false?
choices: It is more common in men than in women
IgG antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor
It is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism
Diffuse hyperplasia, goiter and ophthalmopathy are typical
ex: Graves disease: an IgG autoantibody stimulates the TSH receptor, causing diffuse hyperplasia, goiter and ophthalmopathy. It is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism, women 5 to 1.
why: This is the false one: Graves disease affects women about 5 times as often as men.
This is true: an IgG autoantibody stimulates the TSH receptor, so the gland overproduces.
This is true: Graves disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.
This is true: the whole gland is hyperplastic and enlarged, and Graves ophthalmopathy is part of it.

stem: Which statement about hypopituitarism is false?
choices: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of the posterior pituitary around delivery
Symptoms appear only after about 75 percent of the anterior pituitary is lost
A null cell adenoma makes no hormone but can shut down the normal gland as a mass
A hypothalamic tumor can cause it by stopping the releasing factors
ex: Hypopituitarism appears once about 75 percent of the anterior pituitary is lost. Causes include null cell adenomas, Sheehan syndrome (postpartum ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary) and, less often, a hypothalamic tumor.
why: This is the false one: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary, which is why she can't breastfeed.
This is true: the gland has a large reserve, so about 75 percent must be lost.
This is true: a nonsecretory adenoma causes hypopituitarism by pressing on the normal gland.
This is true: a hypothalamic disorder can stop the releasing factors, a less common cause.

stem: Which statement about pheochromocytoma is true?
choices: Its tumor cells form nests called zellballen
It is a tumor of the adrenal cortex's zona fasciculata
It secretes cortisol, causing attacks of sweating and palpitations
Its attacks bring sweating, palpitations and low blood pressure
ex: Pheochromocytoma: a tumor of the medulla's chromaffin cells that secretes catecholamines, with attacks of sweating, palpitations and hypertension. Rule of 10s; its cells form zellballen.
why: Pheochromocytoma's chromaffin cells grow in nests, the zellballen.
It is a tumor of the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, not the cortex.
It secretes catecholamines; cortisol comes from the zona fasciculata.
The catecholamine surges raise blood pressure: the attacks are hypertensive.

stem: Which statement about neuroblastoma is false?
choices: It is a slow-growing tumor found mostly in adults over 50
About 80 percent of cases are in children under 5
It spreads to bone, liver, lung and lymph nodes
In adults, olfactory neuroblastoma arises in the roof of the nose
ex: Neuroblastoma: very aggressive, 80 percent under age 5, arising along the sympathetic chain (the abdomen most often) and spreading to bone, liver, lung and lymph nodes. Adults get olfactory neuroblastoma in the roof of the nose.
why: This is the false one: neuroblastoma is very aggressive, and about 80 percent of cases are in children under 5.
This is true: neuroblastoma is a tumor of young children.
This is true: those are its sites of spread.
This is true: the adult form, olfactory neuroblastoma, sits in the roof of the nasal cavity.

stem: Which statement about aldosterone and hyperaldosteronism is false?
choices: In Conn syndrome, aldosterone and renin are both high
Renal artery stenosis raises both aldosterone and renin
Aldosterone makes the kidney take back sodium and dump potassium
Heart failure can cause secondary hyperaldosteronism
ex: Aldosterone takes back sodium and dumps potassium. Primary (Conn): aldosterone high, renin low. Secondary (heart failure, renal artery stenosis): aldosterone high and renin high.
why: This is the false one: in Conn syndrome (primary) the high aldosterone suppresses renin, so renin is low.
This is true: in secondary hyperaldosteronism, renin drives the aldosterone, so both are high.
This is true: aldosterone retains sodium and excretes potassium.
This is true: CHF and renal artery stenosis are the lecture's causes of the secondary form.

stem: Which statement about the spermatogonia is true?
choices: Pale type A spermatogonia are the progenitors, with a central nucleolus and no vacuole
Dark type A spermatogonia are the progenitors, with a central nucleolus and no nuclear vacuole
Type B spermatogonia are the reserve stem cells, with a nuclear vacuole
Type B spermatogonia sit in the adluminal compartment, above the tight junctions
ex: Dark type A: the reserve stem cell, with a nuclear vacuole and a peripheral nucleolus. Pale type A: the progenitor, no vacuole and a central nucleolus. Type B spermatogonia become primary spermatocytes, which move into the adluminal compartment.
why: Pale type A cells are the progenitors: no nuclear vacuole and a central nucleolus.
Dark type A cells are the reserve stem cells, with a nuclear vacuole and a peripheral nucleolus.
The reserve stem cells are the dark type A spermatogonia; type B cells go on to become primary spermatocytes.
Spermatogonia, type B included, sit in the basal compartment; primary spermatocytes are the ones that move past the junctions.

stem: Which statement about the testis and its seminiferous tubules is false?
choices: The tubule's epithelium contains Sertoli cells, spermatogenic cells and Leydig cells
Septa running in from the thick tunica albuginea divide the testis into about 250 lobules
Each lobule holds several blind-ended, coiled seminiferous tubules
Peritubular myoid cells lie in the tubule's outer wall
ex: The thick tunica albuginea sends septa in, making about 250 lobules, each with several blind-ended, coiled seminiferous tubules. The wall: connective tissue and peritubular myoid cells. The epithelium: only Sertoli cells and spermatogenic cells. Leydig cells lie between the tubules.
why: This is the false one: the epithelium has only Sertoli cells and spermatogenic cells; Leydig cells sit in the connective tissue between the tubules.
This is true: the septa make about 250 lobules.
This is true: each lobule has several coiled tubules.
This is true: the wall is connective tissue with peritubular myoid cells.

stem: Which statement about the vas deferens and the ducts beyond it is false?
choices: The vas deferens joins the prostate's duct to form the ejaculatory duct
The vas deferens has a thick muscular wall and stereocilia
The testicular artery and pampiniform plexus run in the spermatic cord with the vas
The ejaculatory duct passes through the prostate to the urethra
ex: Vas deferens: straight, a thick muscular wall, stereocilia; it runs in the spermatic cord with the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus. The vas and the seminal vesicle's duct form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate into the urethra.
why: This is the false one: the vas joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.
This is true: a straight duct with a thick muscular wall, lined with stereocilia.
This is true: Dr. Herr said those are the only two other parts of the cord to know.
This is true: the ejaculatory duct runs through the prostate and opens into the urethra.

stem: Which statement about the stages of the ovarian follicle is true?
choices: An early primary follicle has one layer of cuboidal granulosa cells
A primordial follicle has one layer of cuboidal granulosa cells
A late primary follicle already has an antrum filled with liquor folliculi
A Graafian follicle is about 2 mm across and lies deep in the ovary
ex: Primordial: one layer of squamous cells. Early primary: one layer of cuboidal granulosa cells. Late primary: several layers, theca forming. Secondary: liquor folliculi and an antrum. Graafian: about 20 mm, bulging on the ovary.
why: The early primary follicle's single layer has turned cuboidal: these are now granulosa cells.
A primordial follicle's single layer is squamous; cuboidal cells mark the early primary follicle.
Liquor folliculi and an antrum are what make a follicle secondary; the late primary has several layers but no antrum.
A Graafian follicle is about 20 mm and bulges from the surface of the ovary.

stem: Which statement about the vagina and cervix is true?
choices: The vagina's lining is stratified squamous epithelium with no glands
The vagina's lining is simple columnar epithelium with many mucous glands
Lactobacillus turns the vagina's glycogen into acetic acid, which keeps pathogens down
Cervical mucus is thick and viscous at ovulation and watery in pregnancy
ex: Vagina: stratified squamous, no glands; Lactobacillus turns glycogen into lactic acid, which keeps pathogens down. Cervix: mucus-secreting columnar crypts; watery mucus at ovulation, a viscous plug in pregnancy; the transformation zone meets stratified squamous epithelium.
why: Stratified squamous epithelium, and no glands.
Simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium lines the cervical canal, not the vagina, and the vagina has no glands.
Lactobacillus makes lactic acid from the glycogen.
That swaps them: watery at ovulation, a viscous plug in pregnancy.

stem: Which statement about the oocyte's meiosis is false?
choices: The ovulated cell is a secondary oocyte arrested in prophase I
Every follicle in a resting ovary holds a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I
Only fertilization finishes meiosis II, giving an ovum and a second polar body
Unequal cytokinesis gives one large oocyte and one tiny polar body
ex: Primary oocyte: arrested in prophase I in every follicle; the LH surge finishes meiosis I just before ovulation. The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II, and only fertilization finishes meiosis II. Each division is unequal: one big oocyte, one tiny polar body.
why: This is the false one: the ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II; prophase I is where the primary oocyte waits.
This is true: the primary oocyte waits in prophase I until the LH surge.
This is true: without fertilization, meiosis II is never completed.
This is true: nearly all the cytoplasm stays with the oocyte.

stem: Which statement about the hormones around ovulation is false?
choices: Progesterone from the Graafian follicle triggers the LH surge
FSH grows a group of 10 to 12 antral follicles
The LH surge finishes meiosis I just before ovulation
Theca interna cells carry LH receptors and make androgens that become estrogen
ex: FSH grows 10 to 12 antral follicles; LH matures and ovulates the dominant one. Estrogen from the Graafian follicle triggers the LH surge, which finishes meiosis I and leads to rupture. The theca interna has LH receptors and makes androgens, the estrogen precursors.
why: This is the false one: estrogen from the Graafian follicle triggers the LH surge.
This is true: the FSH surge grows 10 to 12 antral follicles, and one becomes dominant.
This is true: the LH surge restarts the primary oocyte's arrested meiosis.
This is true: the theca interna's androgens are the precursors of estrogen.

stem: Which statement about male reproductive lab patterns is true?
choices: Failing testes give low testosterone with high LH and FSH
A failing pituitary gives low testosterone with high LH and FSH
Injected testosterone gives high testosterone with high LH and FSH
Continuous GnRH raises LH and testosterone more than pulses do
ex: Failing testes: low testosterone, high LH and FSH. Failing pituitary: all low. Injected testosterone: high testosterone, low LH and FSH, low sperm count. GnRH works only in pulses.
why: With no testosterone or inhibin to feed back, the pituitary turns LH and FSH up.
A failing pituitary makes everything low: LH, FSH and testosterone.
Injected testosterone suppresses LH and FSH, so the sperm count falls too.
GnRH must pulse; given continuously, it lowers LH and testosterone.

stem: Which statement about 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is true?
choices: The person is XY with testes and Wolffian ducts but has female genitalia
The person is XY with testes, but the Müllerian ducts persist as a uterus
The person is XX with ovaries, and virilizes at puberty
The androgen receptor is mutated, so testosterone has no effect anywhere
ex: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: XY, testes, Wolffian ducts present, no Müllerian ducts, but female external genitalia because DHT builds the penis, scrotum and prostate. Raised as girls, they virilize at puberty, often how it's found.
why: Testosterone still builds the Wolffian structures, but without DHT the external genitalia stay female.
Sertoli AMH still works, so there are no Müllerian ducts and no uterus.
The person is XY with testes; the virilization at puberty is right.
A mutated or absent androgen receptor is androgen insensitivity syndrome, a different condition.

stem: Which statement about the fluids that make up semen is false?
choices: The prostate's PSA forms the clot, and fibrinogen from the seminal vesicles breaks it
The seminal vesicles supply most of the fluid, with fructose for energy
Prostaglandins in the seminal vesicles' fluid cause contractions in the female reproductive tract
Cowper's glands' mucus comes before ejaculation and neutralizes the urethra
ex: Seminal vesicles: 60 to 70 percent of the fluid, fructose, prostaglandins (female tract contractions) and fibrinogen (the clot). Prostate: 20 to 30 percent, thin milky fluid with citrate, calcium and PSA, which breaks the clot. Cowper's glands: clear, alkaline mucus before ejaculation.
why: This is the false one: that swaps them; seminal vesicle fibrinogen forms the clot and the prostate's PSA breaks it down.
This is true: 60 to 70 percent of the fluid, with fructose.
This is true: Dr. Madison taught that the prostaglandins make the female tract contract.
This is true: the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands' clear, alkaline mucus lubricates and neutralizes the urethra first.

stem: Which statement about the hormones of the male reproductive axis is false?
choices: Inhibin from Sertoli cells inhibits FSH at both the hypothalamus and the pituitary
Testosterone feeds back to inhibit GnRH at the hypothalamus and LH at the pituitary
GnRH must pulse; given continuously, it lowers LH and testosterone
LH turns up cholesterol desmolase in Leydig cells, as ACTH does in the adrenal
ex: Testosterone inhibits GnRH (hypothalamus) and LH (pituitary); inhibin from Sertoli cells inhibits FSH at the pituitary only. GnRH must pulse. LH turns up cholesterol desmolase, the rate-limiting step, as ACTH does in the adrenal.
why: This is the false one: inhibin acts at the pituitary only.
This is true: testosterone inhibits both GnRH and LH.
This is true: continuous GnRH shuts the axis down.
This is true: LH controls the rate-limiting step, side-chain cleavage, just as ACTH does in the adrenal.

stem: Which statement about the three estrogens is true?
choices: Estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy, made by the placenta from fetal precursors
Estrone is the main estrogen the ovary makes during a woman's reproductive years
17-beta-estradiol is the estrogen of menopause, made from adrenal DHEA
Estrone in menopause comes from DHEA made by the adrenal zona glomerulosa
ex: 17-beta-estradiol: the main ovarian estrogen. Estrone: the estrogen of menopause, from adrenal DHEA (zona reticularis). Estriol: the estrogen of pregnancy, from fetal 16-OH-DHEA-S in the placenta.
why: Estriol comes from the placenta, built from the fetus's 16-OH-DHEA-S.
The main ovarian estrogen is 17-beta-estradiol; estrone dominates after menopause.
The estrogen of menopause is estrone; 17-beta-estradiol is the main ovarian estrogen.
The DHEA comes from the zona reticularis; the zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone.

stem: Which statement about ovulation is true?
choices: Ovulation comes about 14 days before menses, whatever the cycle's length
The egg is released about 2 to 4 hours after the LH surge
Collagenases strengthen the follicle wall so it can hold the egg until it is released
Prostaglandins lower blood flow to the follicle just before ovulation
ex: Ovulation falls about 14 days before menses. The egg leaves 24 to 36 hours after the LH surge, as collagenases weaken the follicle wall and prostaglandins raise its blood flow.
why: The luteal phase is the fixed part: ovulation falls about 14 days before the next menses.
The egg comes out about 24 to 36 hours after the LH surge.
Collagenases weaken the follicle wall so it can rupture.
Prostaglandins raise blood flow to the follicle.

stem: Which statement about feedback in the female reproductive axis is false?
choices: Progesterone switches to positive feedback once it rises above about 200 pg/mL
Inhibin from the ovary suppresses FSH
Positive feedback is what makes the female axis cyclical
KNDy neurons relay stress, nutrition and inflammation signals to the GnRH neurons
ex: Progesterone gives negative feedback only. Estrogen gives negative feedback, or positive above about 200 pg/mL, and that positive feedback makes the female axis cyclical. Inhibin suppresses FSH. KNDy neurons relay stress, nutrition, metabolism and inflammation to the GnRH neurons.
why: This is the false one: estrogen is the hormone that switches to positive feedback above about 200 pg/mL; progesterone gives negative feedback only.
This is true: the ovary makes inhibin, which holds FSH down.
This is true: the male axis has no positive feedback and is acyclical.
This is true: the GnRH neurons don't sense these directly; the kisspeptin (KNDy) neurons pass them on.

stem: Which statement about the effects of estrogen and progesterone is false?
choices: Progesterone makes the myometrium contract, and estrogen relaxes it
Estrogen makes the cervical mucus watery
Progesterone increases the endometrium's secretions and blood vessels and thickens the mucus
Estrogen drives endometrial growth and lengthens its arteries
ex: Estrogen: endometrial growth, longer arteries, watery mucus, a contracting myometrium. Progesterone: more secretions and vessels, thick mucus, a relaxed myometrium.
why: This is the false one: that swaps them; estrogen makes the myometrium contract and progesterone relaxes it.
This is true: estrogen produces the watery mucus of the follicular phase.
This is true: those are progesterone's luteal-phase effects.
This is true: estrogen rebuilds the endometrium in the proliferative phase.

stem: Insulin clears glucose from the blood into skeletal muscle and fat by moving one transporter from inside the cell to the cell membrane. Which transporter is it?
choices: GLUT4
GLUT1
GLUT2
SGLT2
ex: GLUT4 is the one to know: it waits inside muscle and fat cells until the insulin receptor (a tyrosine kinase) signals it to the membrane. The other GLUTs work without insulin, which is why the brain gets glucose whether or not insulin is around.
why: GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent transporter: the insulin receptor's signal translocates it from the cytoplasm to the membrane of muscle and fat cells.
GLUT1 handles basal glucose uptake and carries glucose across the blood-brain barrier without waiting for insulin.
GLUT2 is one of the insulin-independent transporters (with GLUT1, 3 and 5); it works whether or not insulin is present.
SGLT2 reabsorbs filtered glucose in the kidney; it is the target of the gliflozins, not the transporter insulin moves.

likely.t: Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications

stem: Why does a hemoglobin A1C value reflect a patient's average blood glucose over roughly the past 3 months?
choices: Glucose binds hemoglobin covalently and stays for the red cell's life
Glucose binds hemoglobin reversibly, so the value falls as soon as glucose does
Red cells take glucose in through GLUT4 and hold it until they are replaced
It measures the C-peptide released with each insulin molecule over months
ex: HbA1c is hemoglobin A with a sugar attached to its first amino acid. The higher the glucose, the higher the percentage glycated, and because the bond is covalent the value covers the red cell's life span of about 3 to 4 months.
why: The binding is irreversible and red cells live about 90 to 120 days, so the percentage glycated tracks glucose over that span.
If glucose came off when blood glucose fell, A1C would show only today's level; the professor stressed that A1C does not come down when glucose drops.
GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent transporter of muscle and fat; A1C is glucose bound to the hemoglobin molecule itself.
C-peptide is the marker of the patient's own insulin production, not of average glucose.

stem: True or false: An HbA1c of 6.2 percent is in the diabetic range.
choices: True
False
ex: Diabetes starts at an A1C of 6.5 percent. Normal is under 5.7, and 5.7 to 6.4 is prediabetes, so 6.2 percent is prediabetes.
why: 6.2 percent is below the diabetic cutoff of 6.5 percent; it falls in the prediabetes window of 5.7 to 6.4.
Diabetes begins at 6.5 percent; 6.2 sits in the prediabetes range of 5.7 to 6.4 percent.

stem: True or false: Once someone has prediabetes, progressing to type 2 diabetes is a given.
choices: True
False
ex: Prediabetes is the window between normal and diabetic numbers (A1C 5.7 to 6.4 percent, fasting glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL). It has no symptoms and most people with it don't know, but it can be reversed.
why: The professor said the opposite: it is not a given that prediabetes becomes diabetes.
Prediabetes can be reversed: diet, lifestyle change and weight loss bring many people back to normal numbers.

likely.t: Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications

stem:
Each result below comes from a different patient. Which results fall in the diabetic range?
1. Fasting plasma glucose 118 mg/dL
2. HbA1c 6.7%
3. Glucose 215 mg/dL 2 hours into an oral glucose tolerance test
4. HbA1c 5.9%
choices: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
3 only
ex: Diabetic range: A1C 6.5 percent or higher, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance value of 200 or higher, or a random glucose above 200. A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 and an A1C of 5.7 to 6.4 are prediabetes.
why: It includes 1, which is false: 118 mg/dL is in the prediabetes window of 100 to 125; the diabetic cutoff is 126. It leaves out 2, which is true: an A1C of 6.7 percent is above the 6.5 percent cutoff.

Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: 118 mg/dL is in the prediabetes window of 100 to 125; the diabetic cutoff is 126. Statement 4 is false: 5.9 percent is prediabetes (5.7 to 6.4), not diabetes.
It includes 4, which is false: 5.9 percent is prediabetes (5.7 to 6.4), not diabetes.
It leaves out 2, which is true: an A1C of 6.7 percent is above the 6.5 percent cutoff.

likely.t: Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications

stem: Each of the following is a microvascular complication of diabetes EXCEPT:
choices: Stroke
Neuropathy
Nephropathy
Retinopathy
ex: Microvascular means small vessels: neuropathy, nephropathy and retinopathy. Macrovascular means big vessels: coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease and stroke.
why: Stroke is macrovascular, with coronary artery disease and peripheral vascular disease: it affects the big vessels.
Neuropathy is one of the three microvascular complications the professor called very important to know.
Nephropathy is microvascular; diabetes is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease.
Retinopathy is microvascular and is often how an optometrist first discovers that a patient has diabetes.

likely.t: Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications

stem: True or false: The non-ketotic hyperosmolar state carries a higher mortality than diabetic ketoacidosis.
choices: True
False
ex: Both are acute complications. DKA comes from cells starved of glucose burning fatty acids into ketone bodies; the non-ketotic hyperosmolar state comes from the sheer amount of glucose in the blood and can lead to stupor, coma and death.
why: The professor said the hyperosmolar state is actually more deadly than DKA.
It is the other way around: the non-ketotic hyperosmolar state has the higher mortality.

stem: A patient with no history of diabetes develops hyperglycemia while being treated for Cushing syndrome. According to the lecture, treatment should focus on:
choices: The underlying Cushing syndrome that is causing the hyperglycemia
Lifelong insulin, because new hyperglycemia means type 1 diabetes
Metformin, because it is first-line for any newly found hyperglycemia
A sulfonylurea, to squeeze more insulin out of the pancreas
ex: Pregnancy (gestational diabetes), acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, chronic pancreatitis, cancer and several drugs can raise glucose. That is secondary diabetes: there is a primary cause, and treatment is aimed at it.
why: Secondary diabetes has a primary cause, and the professor said you treat that cause rather than the diabetes.
Type 1 is autoimmune loss of beta cells; hyperglycemia caused by another disease is secondary, not type 1.
Metformin is first-line for type 2 diabetes in an otherwise healthy patient, not for hyperglycemia with a treatable cause.
Stimulating insulin release ignores the cause of the high glucose.

stem: A man without diabetes is treated for a dangerously high potassium (see the Patient Box). Why is dextrose given together with the insulin?
choices: To prevent hypoglycemia while insulin drives potassium into cells
Because dextrose itself is what pumps potassium into the cells
To treat the undiagnosed diabetes that raised his potassium level
To replace glucose he is losing in the urine by osmotic diuresis
ex: Insulin increases cellular potassium uptake through Na/K-ATPase, so it is a standard way to bring down a high potassium, even in people who don't have diabetes. It is given with glucose so the patient doesn't become hypoglycemic.
pbox: 67-year-old man in the emergency department with muscle weakness and an irregular heartbeat
why: Insulin lowers potassium by stimulating Na/K-ATPase uptake into cells; the glucose gives insulin something to clear so blood sugar doesn't crash.
The potassium-lowering effect is insulin's, through Na/K-ATPase; the dextrose is there to protect the blood glucose.
He has no diabetes; here insulin is used only as a potassium-lowering drug.
Glucose lost in the urine is what SGLT2 inhibitors cause; it has nothing to do with this treatment.

stem: A dental patient with repeated periodontal abscesses is sent for blood work (see the Patient Box). Which conclusion do the results best support?
choices: He has diabetes: two criteria agree from the one blood draw
He has prediabetes, so diet and exercise are all he needs
Nothing can be concluded until the glucose is repeated next visit
His values are normal, so the oral findings have another cause
ex: Diagnosis needs two of: A1C 6.5 percent or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more, a 2-hour glucose tolerance value of 200 or more, or a random glucose above 200. Periodontal disease, slow healing, oral infections and dry mouth are the dental signs on the slide, and the dentist may be the first to suspect diabetes.
pbox: 49-year-old man at a dental recall visit
Two periodontal abscesses this year, a slow-healing extraction socket, dry mouth
Always thirsty; gets up at night to urinate
eGFR 88 mL/min; no heart, liver or kidney disease; BMI 27
why: An A1C of 6.5 percent or more plus a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more are two agreeing criteria, enough for a diagnosis from a single draw.
Prediabetes is an A1C of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125; both of his values are above those ranges.
Before A1C, glucose had to be high on two visits; now an A1C and a fasting glucose from the same draw can confirm it.
Normal is an A1C under 5.7 percent and a fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL; his are well above both.

likely.t: Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications

stem: The same patient is otherwise healthy. Which drug is the standard first-line choice for him?
choices: Metformin
Glipizide
Insulin glargine
Sitagliptin
ex: Apart from comorbidities that point elsewhere (a weight problem toward a GLP-1 agonist, heart failure or cardiovascular disease toward an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 agonist), metformin is the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes. Other drugs are added on when it is no longer enough.
pbox: 49-year-old man at a dental recall visit
Two periodontal abscesses this year, a slow-healing extraction socket, dry mouth
Always thirsty; gets up at night to urinate
eGFR 88 mL/min; no heart, liver or kidney disease; BMI 27
why: Metformin is still the first-line drug for a newly diagnosed, otherwise healthy patient with type 2 diabetes.
A sulfonylurea lowers glucose but causes hypoglycemia and weight gain and loses effect over time; it is not first-line.
Insulin is the treatment for type 1 diabetes; he still makes insulin, and type 2 starts with metformin.
A DPP-4 inhibitor is an add-on: expensive, with only modest A1C lowering.

likely.t: Metformin: first-line, mechanism, no effect at normal glucose, GI upset, B12, lactic acidosis, eGFR below 30

stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes is about to sit down to a large, carbohydrate-heavy dinner and needs insulin to cover the rise in glucose after the meal. Which is the best choice?
choices: Insulin aspart
NPH insulin
Insulin glargine
Insulin degludec
ex: Mealtime (bolus) insulin has to start fast: the rapid analogs lispro, aspart and glulisine, or regular insulin. As the professor put it, once you eat you can't wait 2 to 4 hours for NPH to kick in.
why: Aspart is rapid-acting (onset in about 5 to 15 minutes), so given just before the meal it covers the postprandial spike.
NPH takes 2 to 4 hours to start working, far too late for a meal that is about to be eaten.
Glargine is a basal insulin with a slow, steady release over more than 24 hours; it doesn't cover a meal spike.
Degludec is ultra-long-acting (more than 42 hours): basal coverage, not a mealtime dose.

likely.t: Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation

stem: Of these insulins, which one's effect wears off soonest?
choices: Insulin lispro
Regular insulin
NPH insulin
Insulin detemir
ex: Shortest to longest: rapid analogs (lispro, aspart, glulisine), then regular, then NPH, then the long-acting glargine and detemir, then ultra-long degludec. These time profiles decide which insulin is basal and which is used as needed with meals.
why: Lispro is rapid-acting: onset in 5 to 15 minutes and a total duration of about 4 hours, the shortest here.
Regular (short-acting) insulin peaks around 3 hours and is gone by about 8 hours, longer than the rapid analogs.
NPH is intermediate-acting: protamine slows its absorption so it lasts longer than regular insulin.
Detemir is a long-acting basal insulin.

likely.t: Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation

stem: In a basal-bolus regimen, which insulin is typically injected once a day, for example at night, to mimic the body's own background insulin?
choices: Insulin glargine
Insulin glulisine
Regular insulin
Inhaled insulin (Afrezza)
ex: Basal insulin runs all day whether or not the patient eats; bolus insulin is taken as needed (PRN) before each meal and skipped if the meal is skipped.
why: Glargine releases slowly and steadily, with no real peak, and lasts more than 24 hours: the classic once-daily basal insulin.
Glulisine is rapid-acting, a mealtime (bolus) insulin.
Regular insulin peaks around 3 hours and is gone by about 8; it is used before meals.
Afrezza starts working within a minute or two, an ultra-fast mealtime insulin.

likely.t: Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation

stem: What does the protamine in NPH insulin do?
choices: It slows absorption from the injection site, so insulin lasts longer
It speeds absorption so the insulin can be given right before meals
It protects insulin from DPP-4 so the insulin can be taken by mouth
It acidifies the solution so the insulin can be mixed with any other
ex: NPH = neutral protamine Hagedorn: neutral pH, protamine to slow absorption, and Hagedorn, the researcher. It was the first change made to lengthen insulin's action, so patients needed fewer injections.
why: Hagedorn added the protein protamine so injected insulin is released slowly, turning a short-acting insulin into an intermediate one.
Faster release is what the rapid analogs (lispro, aspart, glulisine) were modified for; protamine does the opposite.
DPP-4 breaks down incretins, not insulin, and no insulin is swallowed; the one non-injected insulin is inhaled Afrezza.
The N stands for neutral: the preparation is neither acidic nor basic.

stem: True or false: Regular insulin and NPH can be bought at a pharmacy without a prescription.
choices: True
False
ex: The professor stressed it: the two older human insulins, regular (Humulin R, Novolin R) and NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N), are sold without a prescription to patients who know how to use them. The analogs are not.
why: These two older human insulins are sold without a prescription; the professor said you should know that.
They are the exception: regular and NPH are available without a prescription, though only these two.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Afrezza is an inhaled insulin that starts acting within a few minutes.
2. Insulin glargine has a sharp peak about 3 hours after injection.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Afrezza, inhaled, is the fastest insulin (a minute or two). The sharp peak around 3 hours belongs to regular insulin; glargine releases slowly and evenly with no real peak, which is what makes it a basal insulin.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the peak around 3 hours (gone by about 8) is regular insulin; glargine has a slow, flat release lasting more than 24 hours.
Statement 1 is true, not false: it is given by inhalation and its action sets in within one to two minutes.

Statement 1 is true: it is given by inhalation and its action sets in within one to two minutes. Statement 2 is false: the peak around 3 hours (gone by about 8) is regular insulin; glargine has a slow, flat release lasting more than 24 hours.

Statement 1 is true, not false: it is given by inhalation and its action sets in within one to two minutes. Statement 2 is false, not true: the peak around 3 hours (gone by about 8) is regular insulin; glargine has a slow, flat release lasting more than 24 hours.

likely.t: Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation

stem: Each of the following is an adverse effect of insulin EXCEPT:
choices: Weight loss
Hypoglycemia
Lipohypertrophy at the injection site
Lipoatrophy at the injection site
ex: Insulin's adverse effects: hypoglycemia, weight gain, transient worsening of retinopathy, and lipoatrophy or lipohypertrophy at the injection site.
why: Insulin is anabolic, so it causes weight gain, not weight loss.
Hypoglycemia is insulin's main adverse effect, shared by every drug that raises insulin release.
Fat can build up at a repeatedly used injection site; it is on the list.
Fat can also waste away at an injection site; it is on the list too.

stem: True or false: Starting insulin can cause a temporary worsening of diabetic retinopathy before it improves.
choices: True
False
ex: Transient deterioration of retinopathy is a listed adverse effect: most people with diabetes already have some eye disease, and starting insulin may make it worse for a while before it gets better.
why: Transient worsening of retinopathy is on the list of insulin's adverse effects, with hypoglycemia, weight gain and injection-site changes.
It is a listed adverse effect: eye complications can worsen for a while after insulin is started, then improve.

stem: During a scaling and root planing appointment, a patient with type 1 diabetes becomes sweaty and shaky (see the Patient Box). What should the dental team do first?
choices: Give her orange juice, regular soda or glucose tablets by mouth
Give her an extra dose of lispro to bring her glucose back to normal
Finish the scaling quickly, then recheck her glucose afterward
Give intranasal glucagon before trying any food or drink
ex: Sweating, shaking, anxiety and confusion with a glucose of 52 mg/dL is hypoglycemia. A patient who is awake and can swallow gets fast sugar by mouth (orange juice, regular soda, glucose tablets); glucagon is for emergencies.
pbox: 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, 9:00 am appointment for scaling and root planing
Glargine 18 units at bedtime; lispro before each meal
Took her lispro at 7:30 am, then skipped breakfast to make the appointment
Sweaty, shaky and anxious, a little confused but answering questions; fingerstick glucose 52 mg/dL
why: She is awake and can swallow, so fast sugar by mouth is the first step the lecture gives for hypoglycemia.
Insulin lowers glucose further; her symptoms come from too much insulin for the food she has eaten.
Hypoglycemia can progress to collapse; it is treated as soon as it is recognized, not after the procedure.
Glucagon is the emergency drug for a patient who can't take sugar by mouth; she is alert and can drink.

likely.t: Hypoglycemia in the dental chair: fast sugar by mouth if awake, glucagon in an emergency

stem: Which of her insulins most likely caused this episode?
choices: Lispro, a rapid-acting insulin taken with no meal to cover
Glargine, because its effect peaks sharply about 10 hours after a dose
Glargine, because basal insulin should be skipped on any day she fasts
Neither: like metformin, insulin has no effect once glucose is normal
ex: In basal-bolus therapy the basal insulin (glargine) runs all day regardless of meals, while the bolus (lispro) is taken only when eating. Taking the bolus and skipping the meal leaves insulin with no glucose to match.
pbox: 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, 9:00 am appointment for scaling and root planing
Glargine 18 units at bedtime; lispro before each meal
Took her lispro at 7:30 am, then skipped breakfast to make the appointment
Sweaty, shaky and anxious, a little confused but answering questions; fingerstick glucose 52 mg/dL
why: Lispro starts in 5 to 15 minutes and lasts about 4 hours, so the 7:30 dose was fully active during her appointment, with no breakfast to match.
Glargine has a slow, steady release with no real peak; it mimics background insulin.
The basal dose is taken whether or not she eats; it is the mealtime (PRN) dose that depends on eating.
Having no effect at normal glucose is metformin's property; insulin lowers glucose whatever the starting level, which is why hypoglycemia is its main adverse effect.

stem: Before she can drink anything, she becomes unresponsive and can no longer swallow. Which is the drug of choice now?
choices: Glucagon, by injection or as a nasal spray
Regular insulin given IV together with dextrose
Pramlintide injected under the skin before a meal
Acarbose, to slow the breakdown of carbohydrate
ex: In an emergency, the drug of choice for hypoglycemia is glucagon, which raises glucose from the liver. Nasal glucagon is given like nasal naloxone, so anyone can give it quickly.
pbox: 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, 9:00 am appointment for scaling and root planing
Glargine 18 units at bedtime; lispro before each meal
Took her lispro at 7:30 am, then skipped breakfast to make the appointment
Sweaty, shaky and anxious, a little confused but answering questions; fingerstick glucose 52 mg/dL
why: Glucagon is the emergency treatment; it comes as a powder kit mixed for injection, a stable liquid for injection, or a nasal form.
Insulin with glucose is the treatment for a high potassium, not for hypoglycemia; insulin would lower her glucose further.
Pramlintide is an amylin analog given before meals; with insulin it can cause hypoglycemia, not treat it.
Acarbose blocks carbohydrate digestion, the opposite of what she needs, and she can't swallow.

likely.t: Hypoglycemia in the dental chair: fast sugar by mouth if awake, glucagon in an emergency

stem: Put the steps of sulfonylurea action in order, from the drug to insulin release.
steps: The drug binds the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) on the beta cell
Potassium is trapped inside and the membrane depolarizes
Voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium flows in
Insulin already made in the beta cell is released by exocytosis
ex: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides both close the beta cell's ATP-sensitive potassium channel. Trapped potassium depolarizes the cell, calcium channels open, and the calcium influx triggers exocytosis of stored insulin.

likely.t: Secretagogues: the K-ATP channel mechanism, the need for working beta cells (C-peptide), low durability, sulfonylurea warnings

stem: A man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has been on insulin for 6 years (see the Patient Box). What does his C-peptide result tell his physician?
choices: His beta cells no longer make insulin; what is measured is injected
His beta cells make plenty of insulin, but his tissues resist it
His A1C is falsely high because C-peptide binds to hemoglobin
He makes insulin, but the test can't detect it while he injects
ex: Beta cells make proinsulin, which is cleaved into insulin plus C-peptide in equimolar amounts. An insulin level can't separate injected from natural insulin; C-peptide can. With time, a person with type 2 diabetes can stop making insulin, as in type 1.
pbox: Insulin glargine and insulin aspart for the last 6 years; metformin
30 µIU/mL, drawn 2 hours after his usual morning aspart
Undetectable (below 0.1 ng/mL; normal fasting about 0.5 to 2)
why: Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts and injected insulin carries none, so no C-peptide means no insulin of his own.
If his beta cells were still making insulin, C-peptide would be present in amounts equal to that insulin.
C-peptide plays no part in A1C; it is glucose that binds hemoglobin covalently.
That is the point of the test: an insulin level can't tell his insulin from the injected kind, but C-peptide comes only from his own proinsulin.

likely.t: Secretagogues: the K-ATP channel mechanism, the need for working beta cells (C-peptide), low durability, sulfonylurea warnings

stem: His physician considers adding another drug. Which would be expected to have essentially no effect in him?
choices: Glipizide
Dapagliflozin

ex: Anaplastic carcinoma: about 10 percent of thyroid cancers, ages 60 to 80, often in areas of endemic goiter, a rapidly fatal neck mass that invades cartilage, skin and muscle. It has lost its differentiation and may even lose its thyroid markers.
why: Older age, endemic goiter, a mass growing over weeks to months and undifferentiated cells are anaplastic carcinoma.
It can invade the thyroid cartilage, but it keeps its follicular differentiation and has a mean age of about 50.
Medullary carcinoma forms neuroendocrine nests with amyloid and stains for calcitonin.
Papillary carcinoma is slow growing, in younger patients, with recognizable papillae and nuclei.

likely.t: Thyroid development, follicular adenoma and anaplastic carcinoma

stem: Why does Dr. Dababneh treat a new biopsy diagnosis of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma as an emergency?
choices: Without a targetable mutation such as BRAF it is rapidly fatal, so molecular testing must start at once
It is often multifocal, so the opposite lobe has to be removed before the tumor can seed it
It arises from the C cells and may signal an inherited RET syndrome that the family needs to know about
It is well differentiated, so a hemithyroidectomy done right away will cure it before it spreads
ex: Most patients with anaplastic carcinoma die quickly unless the tumor carries a mutation a targeted drug can hit, such as BRAF. So the pathologist tells the clinicians at once and sends the tissue straight for molecular testing.
why: Most patients die unless the tumor has a mutation a drug can target, so he calls the clinicians and sends it for molecular testing right away.
Multifocality is papillary carcinoma's issue, handled by a total thyroidectomy, not an emergency.
That is medullary carcinoma; anaplastic carcinoma is undifferentiated.
It is the opposite, undifferentiated; a hemithyroidectomy is the operation for follicular carcinoma.

likely.t: Thyroid development, follicular adenoma and anaplastic carcinoma

stem: Match each thyroid carcinoma to the feature that best identifies it.
pairs: RAS mutation; spreads through blood vessels
RET mutation; arises from C cells
Undifferentiated; a rapidly fatal neck mass
ex: The lecture's sorting rule: BRAF-like papillary cancers spread by lymphatics, RAS-like follicular cancers by blood vessels, medullary carcinoma is the RET-driven C-cell tumor, and anaplastic carcinoma has lost its differentiation and kills quickly.

likely.t: Papillary vs follicular carcinoma: BRAF/lymphatics/multifocal/total thyroidectomy vs RAS/blood/invasion/hemithyroidectomy

stem: Low serum calcium triggers PTH release. Which set of actions does PTH have on the kidney?
choices: More calcium reabsorbed, less phosphate reabsorbed, more 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D made
More calcium reabsorbed, more phosphate reabsorbed, less 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D made
Less calcium reabsorbed, less phosphate reabsorbed, more 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D made
More sodium reabsorbed, more potassium excreted, more 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D made
ex: PTH raises serum calcium through the kidney (keep calcium, dump phosphate, make 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D) and the bone (more turnover). The rising calcium then switches PTH off: negative feedback.
why: PTH holds on to calcium, dumps phosphate and turns on active vitamin D, which all push serum calcium up.
PTH makes the kidney dump phosphate, not keep it, and it increases active vitamin D rather than lowering it.
Losing calcium in the urine would lower serum calcium, the opposite of what PTH is released to do.
Keeping sodium and dumping potassium is aldosterone's action on the kidney, not PTH's.

stem: Which statement about the fragments of PTH in the blood is accurate?
choices: N-terminal fragments are biologically active, last minutes and are broken down by the liver and kidney
C-terminal fragments are biologically active, last minutes and are broken down by the liver and kidney
N-terminal fragments are biologically inactive, last several hours and are cleared by glomerular filtration
C-terminal fragments are biologically active, last several hours and are cleared by glomerular filtration
ex: Intact PTH and its N-terminal fragments do the work and last only minutes; C-terminal fragments are inactive, last hours and are cleared by glomerular filtration. That short half-life is why PTH can be measured during surgery to confirm the gland is out.
why: The active end of PTH is short-lived and is metabolized by the liver and kidney.
The C-terminal fragments are the inactive ones; the N-terminal end is the part that acts.
That describes the C-terminal fragments: inactive, long-lived and filtered by the kidney.
C-terminal fragments do last hours and are filtered, but they are biologically inactive.

stem: Dr. Dababneh's rule of thumb: subtract a person's age from 100 to get the expected percent of cells in a normal parathyroid, the rest being fat. A gland from a 65-year-old is about 80 percent cells with very little fat. How is it best read?
choices: Hypercellular for the patient's age, which fits a hyperfunctioning gland
Normal for the patient's age, because parathyroid fat shrinks as people age
Hypocellular for the patient's age, which fits hypoparathyroidism
Normal at any age, since the ratio of fat to cells stays the same
ex: A young adult's parathyroid is mostly cells; a 70-year-old's is about 70 percent fat and 30 percent cells. A middle-aged or older gland at 70 to 80 percent cells is hypercellular and may be hyperfunctioning.
why: At 65 the gland should be about 35 percent cells; 80 percent is far too cellular, the picture of an adenoma or hyperplasia.
Parathyroid fat increases with age; an older gland should be mostly fat, not mostly cells.

stem: Which best defines primary hyperparathyroidism?
choices: PTH secretion that is inappropriately high for the serum calcium, with no known stimulus driving it
PTH secretion raised in response to chronically low serum calcium, most often from renal failure
Normal or high PTH secretion with target organs that fail to respond, so serum calcium stays low
PTH secretion too low for the serum calcium, most often after the glands are removed with the thyroid
ex: Primary means the parathyroid itself is the problem (adenoma, hyperplasia or carcinoma), so PTH and calcium are both high. Secondary means something else, such as renal failure or a lack of calcium or vitamin D, is driving the glands.
why: That is the slide's definition: the gland itself is overactive.
That is secondary hyperparathyroidism: the glands are responding to a disease that lowers calcium.
That is pseudohypoparathyroidism, end-organ resistance to PTH.
That is hypoparathyroidism, which causes low calcium.

stem: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, and about how often is it the cause?

Chief cell hyperplasia of all four glands, in about 80 to 90 percent of cases
A solitary parathyroid adenoma, in about 10 to 15 percent of cases
Parathyroid carcinoma, in about 10 to 15 percent of cases

why: Adenoma is the most common cause by far, 80 to 90 percent.
Hyperplasia is the second cause, about 10 to 15 percent of cases.

stem: The classic triad of primary hyperparathyroidism, which Dr. Dababneh remembered as "stones, bones and groans," is best listed as which?
choices: Renal calculi, osteitis fibrosa cystica and neuromuscular abnormalities
Renal calculi, basal ganglia calcification and tetany with convulsions
Cataracts, dental root hypoplasia and laryngospasm
Short metacarpals and metatarsals, short stature and developmental anomalies

These are the features of pseudohypoparathyroidism.

1, 2 and 5

stem: A patient has high calcium and high PTH. How is a parathyroid adenoma told apart from primary chief cell hyperplasia?
choices: By anatomy: one enlarged gland means adenoma, several enlarged glands mean hyperplasia
By labs: hyperplasia raises PTH and calcium, while an adenoma raises PTH alone
By labs: an adenoma pushes calcium over 13, while hyperplasia keeps it under 13
By histology alone: an adenoma is full of fat, while hyperplasia has little fat
ex: Adenoma and hyperplasia both cause high PTH and hypercalcemia, so the diagnosis is anatomic: a single enlarged gland versus several. Adenomas in all four glands are very rare, so four enlarged glands is most likely hyperplasia.
why: Labs can't separate them, so the number of enlarged glands decides; an adenoma is a solitary lesion.

stem: Which finding most strongly suggests parathyroid carcinoma rather than an adenoma?
choices: Calcium over 13 with an ill-defined neck mass stuck to the thyroid and esophagus
A single well-defined lower gland weighing 0.6 g, rimmed by normal fatty parathyroid
All four glands enlarged, with a combined weight of about 2 g
Mildly high calcium found on routine labs in a patient who feels well

stem: True or false: Most patients with primary hyperparathyroidism today come to attention because of kidney stones or bone disease.

False

stem: True or false: In primary chief cell hyperplasia, the enlarged parathyroid glands contain more stromal fat than normal.
choices: True
False
