stem: In a classic bilateral neck exploration, the surgeon finds all four parathyroid glands enlarged. What is the usual next step?
choices: Remove three and a half glands and leave half a gland to keep calcium in balance
Remove the largest gland, send it to pathology and biopsy the other three
Remove all four glands, since every enlarged gland is a neoplasm
Remove only the two lower glands, since the lower glands are the ones involved most often
ex: One enlarged gland: presumed adenoma, remove it and biopsy a grossly normal gland. Several enlarged: presumed hyperplasia, remove three and a half. Removed tissue can even be saved and re-implanted elsewhere in the body, where it still works.
why: Several enlarged glands means presumed hyperplasia, so three and a half come out and half stays.
That is the plan for a single enlarged gland, a presumed adenoma: remove it and biopsy a normal one.
Hyperplasia is not necessarily neoplastic, and removing all four would leave no PTH at all.
Lower glands are favored by adenoma, a single-gland disease; four enlarged glands is hyperplasia.

stem: Before surgery she has a sestamibi scan. How is the scan best read?
choices: One hyperfunctioning gland, most likely an adenoma, located before surgery
Hyperplasia of all four glands, since uptake was seen everywhere at first
Parathyroid carcinoma, since the tracer stayed in the gland for 2 hours
A failed scan, since the tracer should have cleared from every gland by 2 hours
ex: Sestamibi is the preoperative localization study: at 15 minutes everything lights up; at 2 hours only the hyperfunctioning tissue still holds the tracer. Finding the single adenoma ahead of time is what allows a small, focused incision.
pbox: Uptake throughout the thyroid and parathyroid region
One bright spot remains, below the left lobe of the thyroid
why: Only hyperfunctioning tissue holds the tracer at 2 hours, so one lit spot is a single overactive gland.
Uptake everywhere is the normal early image at 15 minutes; only one spot persisted at 2 hours.
Holding tracer marks a hyperfunctioning gland, not invasion; carcinoma is judged by calcium, size and invasion.
Tracer clearing from normal tissue while one spot stays lit is exactly the expected positive result.

stem: The surgeon removes the left lower gland through a small incision and checks PTH. How should the result be read?
choices: The operation worked: PTH fell by more than half after the gland came out
The operation failed: PTH is still above the upper limit of normal
The result can't be read yet: PTH takes several hours to fall after removal
The operation failed: the surgeon must have removed fat, so the other three glands must come out
ex: Effective surgery means PTH falls more than 50 percent after the enlarged gland is removed, with results in 15 to 20 minutes. This works only because intact PTH has a half-life of minutes.
pbox: 58-year-old woman, single adenoma localized by sestamibi
Focused removal of the left lower parathyroid gland
why: A drop of more than 50 percent within 15 to 20 minutes confirms the hyperfunctioning gland is out.
The test asks for a fall of more than 50 percent, not a normal value; 150 to 70 is about a 53 percent drop.
Active PTH lasts only minutes; the hours-long half-life belongs to the inactive C-terminal fragments.
If PTH had not dropped, the surgeon may have taken fat; here it did drop by more than half.

stem: A 61-year-old man on dialysis for chronic renal failure has calcium 8.1 mg/dL (8.5-10.5) and PTH 420 pg/mL (10-65). At surgery, all four parathyroids are enlarged. Which best explains his glands?
choices: Secondary hyperparathyroidism: chronic low calcium from renal failure drives all four glands to grow
Primary hyperparathyroidism from chief cell hyperplasia, which enlarges all four glands without a stimulus
Pseudohypoparathyroidism: his kidneys resist PTH, so the glands make more and more of it
Parathyroid carcinoma, since PTH is more than six times the upper limit
ex: Renal failure is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism: chronic hypocalcemia keeps the glands stimulated until they are all hyperplastic. Its features resemble primary disease but are less severe; surgery, when needed, is a three-and-a-half gland parathyroidectomy. Primary chief cell hyperplasia also enlarges all four glands, but it raises calcium; his is low, so something is driving the glands, and here it is his renal failure.
why: Renal failure is the most common cause, and the glands enlarge because low calcium keeps stimulating them.
Primary disease raises calcium; his is low, and his renal failure is a known stimulus.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is diagnosed only after renal failure is ruled out, and he has renal failure.
Carcinoma brings very high calcium, over 13, not low calcium.

stem: A patient's secondary hyperparathyroidism is traced to vitamin D deficiency. According to Dr. Dababneh, what matters most?
choices: Treating the vitamin D deficiency, after which calcium and PTH return to normal on their own
Finding the one enlarged gland on a sestamibi scan and removing it through a small incision
Giving glucocorticoids so that negative feedback switches the overactive parathyroids off
Removing all four parathyroid glands right away so that no more PTH can be made
ex: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a response to disease (renal failure, calcium or vitamin D deficiency). Surgery, if needed, is a three-and-a-half gland parathyroidectomy, but the most important step is fixing the cause.
why: He stressed solving the primary issue: once it is fixed, calcium and the parathyroids return to normal.
A single hyperfunctioning gland is the adenoma of primary disease; secondary disease involves all the glands.
Glucocorticoid feedback is the treatment for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, working through ACTH.
Even when surgery is done, half a gland is left behind; and the first job is the cause.

stem: Which of these are causes of hypoparathyroidism given in the lecture? Select all that apply.

Thymic aplasia in DiGeorge syndrome
Autoimmune hereditary polyglandular deficiency syndrome
Chronic renal failure
A solitary parathyroid adenoma
ex: Hypoparathyroidism has three listed causes: surgical (thyroidectomy), congenital absence (thymic aplasia, DiGeorge syndrome) and autoimmune (hereditary polyglandular deficiency syndrome). Renal failure and adenoma both raise PTH.

stem: Using "salt, sugar, sex," a hormone-making lesion confined to the innermost zone of the adrenal cortex would most likely cause which picture?

Granulosa cells keep secreting oocyte maturation inhibitor into it

Fibroblasts lay down collagen as a corpus luteum dies, forming a corpus albicans.

stem: What best explains why her antibiotic course could lead to this?

stem: A person with androgen insensitivity syndrome is XY, has testes and has female external genitalia. Using the lecture's 4 G's of sexual differentiation, which layers are male in this person?

ex: The 4 G's: genetic sex (XY or XX), gonadal sex (testes or ovaries), phenotypic or genital sex (penis or vagina) and gender (identity, a person's internal sense of their own gender, which can't be read from these findings). stem: In a male fetus, which hormone, from which cells, makes the ducts that would otherwise form the female internal structures regress?

stem: Sertoli cells form tight junctions with one another to create the blood-testis barrier. What is the main purpose of this barrier?

It keeps testosterone in the tubule by binding it to androgen-binding protein

Their other jobs (nourishing sperm, secreting fluid and androgen-binding protein, spermiation) are separate functions of the same cell.

likely.t: Sertoli versus Leydig cells: where each sits, FSH versus LH, what each makes (ABP, inhibin, aromatase, AMH versus testosterone) and the blood-testis barrier

stem: A man wades into a cold lake. What happens to his testes and scrotum, and why?

5-alpha-reductase in peripheral tissues
Conversion of adrenal androgens into testosterone

stem: A man is given GnRH continuously instead of in pulses. What happens?
